The linoleum under my bare feet is cold, a crack running along the edge where the floorboard shifted last winter, a brown stain from when I spilled root beer last July that never came out. Dust motes dance in the slant of October sun hitting the kitchen table, the window has a spiderweb in the corner, tiny spider sitting in the middle, I don’t bother to kill it. The wood stove is going, just a little, so the air smells like pine and old ash, screen door propped open creaks when the wind hits it, carries that sweet-sour smell of fermenting apples from the orchard down the road—like old cider, like something left out too long but still good, like the way my grandma’s house used to smell in fall.

I don’t decide what to do first. I just stand there for a minute, watching the lake through the window, mist so thick the far shore is just a blur of burnt orange and brown, like the maples are bleeding into the fog. A loon calls, high and thin, makes my chest feel soft, like I’m missing something I didn’t know I had. I shiver a little even though the sun hits my shoulders through the glass.

Then I remember The Hobbit. It’s on the couch, spine cracked so bad it falls open to the part where Bilbo meets Gollum, pages stained with coffee and apple juice from last year, cover half torn off where I tried to tape it back with packing tape that’s yellowed now, the tape peeling at the edges. I pick it up, sit on the couch, cushion under my right hip has a hole where the stuffing came out, I shift, book falls open to the wrong page, the one where the dwarves are singing about gold. I don’t care. I just stare at the words for a minute, then put the book down on the couch.

I decide to make cinnamon rolls. No recipe. Dump flour and sugar and yeast into a bowl, mix with my hands, dough is lumpy, sticky, gets under my nails, I wipe it on my jeans, leave a white streak. Don’t measure cinnamon, dump a whole bunch in, so the filling is bright orange, roll the dough up wrong, uneven, some rolls too big, some too small, one falls apart when I put it on the pan. Put them in the oven, forget to set a timer. When I remember they’re in there, the edges are black, middle is still gooey. Take the pan out with a towel, burn my thumb on the edge, curse under my breath, lick the cinnamon off the burn, it’s sweet and hot.

Take one of the rolls, the middle part that’s not burnt, go out to the porch. Swing is there, frayed wool blanket draped over the arm, smells like mothballs and pine and old dog, I think, from when my old lab used to sleep on it. Sit on the swing, rock it, creaks loud, mist is so thick it makes my cheeks cold even though the sun is warm on my back. Eat the roll, cinnamon is too much, sugar is sticky on my fingers, I wipe them on my jeans too, leave a brown streak.

Then I see the geese. So low I can hear their wings beating, mist so thick I can barely see their bodies, just the V shape against the gray, honk loud and rough, I wave even though they can’t see me, even though they’re just flying over the lake.

Loon calls again. Put the half-eaten roll down on the porch rail, wrap the blanket around my shoulders, rock the swing. Don’t think about anything. Don’t think about work, don’t think about bills, don’t think about anyone needing anything. Just listen to the loon, the creak of the swing, the wind carrying the fermenting apples, the mist settling on my hair, making it damp. Fall asleep without meaning to, head lolling to the side, the Hobbit still on the couch inside, the burnt rolls on the kitchen table, the spider still in the window, no one needing anything, no deadlines, nothing.

I’m a sack of sun-warmed tangerine, heavy and soft, my belly pressing so deep into the couch arm that the oak’s hard edge is a distant hum under the frayed cream wool. The wool is scratchy at the edges—loose threads catching on the pink pads of my front paw, a tiny tickle that makes my toe twitch, but I don’t move. The sun hits the crown of my head, the orange fur there so hot I can feel it through the thick, slightly matted coat, warm enough to make my ears droop half-closed against the golden blur of light.

The TV hums low, a wash of purple and green bleeding into the room—*The Wild Thornberrys Movie*, I think, though I don’t care. The dialogue is muffled: Eliza’s sharp kid’s voice, Nigel’s posh accent fading, a soft snippet of the theme song that sounds like it’s coming through a pillow. It’s just background, like the thud-thud-thud of the golden retriever’s tail in the next room. That thud is steady, sometimes pausing for a second when the dog sniffs something—maybe a sock, maybe a crumb—then picking up again, soft and rhythmic, like a lullaby I don’t have to sing.

The cheese puffs are right there, on the scuffed oak coffee table, the smell hitting my nose so hard it makes my whiskers twitch. Salty, cheesy, a little stale but perfect, like the best thing in the world. I can reach them with my paw, if I want—my front leg is long enough, stretched out just a little—but I don’t. The effort is too much. The wool smells like old lavender detergent, the couch smells like warm wood and a faint whiff of lemon polish from when the human scrubbed it last, the air smells like nothing else, just sun and cheese and quiet.

I licked a crumb off my paw a minute ago, so there’s a faint cheesy-salty taste on my tongue, and a tiny scratchy taste of wool fiber I accidentally licked, but it’s not bad. My chest rumbles, soft, a purr that’s too lazy to get loud—half-asleep, half-alive, all warm. My hind leg is splayed out a little, too heavy to tuck tight, the fur there soft and thick, sun-warmed too. The light shifts a little, and I shift, just a little, so the wool bunches under my chest, and the thud-thud-thud keeps going, and the TV keeps humming, and I’m so heavy, so warm, so sleepy, that nothing matters except this. This is the best thing. This is all I need.

Then the knock: soft, slippery, like wet paws on oak.

Elara trundles down the spiral stairs, the shortbread tray’s parchment crinkling, and yanks open the door. Four selkies stand on the threshold, their wool clothes soaked through, sealskins slung over their arms (dark gray, silver, pale blue, speckled like starfish) and their hair stuck to their cheekbones. The smell hits first: brine sharp enough to sting the sinuses, mixed with wild sea lavender—like the tide pools near the lighthouse after a storm. The lead selkie, with a silver shell stud in her left ear, bows slightly: “Apologies for the water. We heard about your shortbread from a local gannet. Got lost. Can’t go back to the water till the storm calms. And we need to dry our skins—they’ll rot if left out.” Polite. So polite it makes Elara’s throat tight.

10:22 PM: The squelch.

Each step up the stone stairs is a wet, gurgling suck—like the ocean is trying to pull the lighthouse down. Mabel, retired fisherman and weekly lemon tea regular, yells from the landing: “ELARA! I LEFT MY THERMOS IN THE CAR, IT’S COLD BUT STILL DRINKABLE—AND I GOT A CRAB IN MY RAIN BOOT, DON’T LET IT PINCH YOU!” Her oilskin jacket has a tear at the elbow, her boots have a hole in the toe (water leaks out with every step, leaving tiny puddles), and she doesn’t bat an eye at the selkies—she’s seen weirder things (a mermaid who stole her bait bucket, a ghost who fixed her net). She grabs the selkies’ skins by the edge of their fur (smelling that same brine-lavender) and heaves them up to the second-floor drying rack—using her jacket to hold them so she doesn’t get wet.

10:25 PM: The shortbread heist.

Elara brings the tray down to the first floor to serve the selkies, the caramel oozing so hot it glows. Her tabby Clam—named for his habit of hiding in dark, tight spots—scampers out from under the stairs, jumps onto the tray, and takes a bite of the corner of a still-warm square. Caramel oozes onto his tabby paw, and he scampers under the lighthouse control panel (bolted shut, with a crack in the glass from a mixing bowl drop last month) and hides. Elara hisses, “CLAM, THAT’S FOR THE SELKIES!” but she can’t reach him—her hand won’t fit in the narrow gap, and Clam hisses back, territorial over his stolen bite.

10:38 PM: The bulb cuts out.

The storm slams a power line. The lighthouse goes dark, save for faint bioluminescent flecks in the selkies’ hair (like plankton) and the warm, caramel-scented glow of the shortbread. Mabel fumbles for her phone flashlight, which illuminates water dripping from the selkies’ hair onto the stone floor, making tiny puddles that reflect the light. The howl is so loud it feels like the lighthouse is breathing in and out.

10:42 PM: The bulb flickers back on.

Bright, white, spinning once.

And the selkies do it.

All four step forward, raise their left hands (each has a tiny urchin scar on the palm), wave twice, tap their left feet twice, then bow slightly. Elara freezes. That’s her treat signal. When she was 7, scared of the dark, she’d leave shortbread crumbs on the lighthouse rail for the “sea cats” she thought she saw. She’d wave left twice, tap left twice, to say I’m here, I’m not scary. The selkies watched her every weekend for a year. No one else would recognize that specific, stupid, kid-made signal. Only Elara.

10:45 PM: The cozy chaos peaks.

Elara serves the selkies shortbread, Mabel pours cold lemon tea into chipped mugs (Elara’s favorite has a lighthouse on it, chipped at the rim), and Mabel pulls the crab out of her rain boot—tucks it into a bucket of seawater by the door (for cleaning fish) and says, “That little guy can stay till the storm passes.” The selkies eat slowly, their teeth slightly sharp, licking caramel off their fingers. Clam finally scampers out from under the control panel, his paw still sticky with caramel, and jumps into Elara’s lap, purring so loud it drowns out the radio.

10:58 PM: The sealskins are dry—Mabel hung them with seashell clothespins (Elara’s grandma’s). The shortbread tray is almost empty.

11:02 PM: The storm calms. The selkies slip their skins over their clothes—their human features soften, their hair turns to fur, their shoulders hunch like they’re getting ready to dive. They thank Elara and Mabel, apologize again for the water, and slip out the door—you hear the soft splash of their dive into the ocean.

Elara looks at the control panel. Clam left a sticky caramel paw print on the red emergency button. She laughs. Mabel says, “You should sell that shortbread to the selkies. They’d pay you in pearls.”

The 45-minute shift ends with a sticky cat, a bucket with a crab, and a secret only the lighthouse keeper and the sea knows.

I smelled the fryer before I saw the stand—thick, warm, nutty fumes curling over the crowd, cutting through the smell of cut hay and fried pickles. When I rounded the corner, the tabby was already there: scruffy, half-torn ear, tail held high like a flag, bolting out from the maze with a kid hot on its heels. The kid was maybe six, in overalls caked with mud on the knee, a crumpled blue cotton candy stick clutched so tight their knuckles were white, yelling “WAIT! I PROMISE I WON’T DROP IT!” They skidded to a stop right in front of the stand’s wooden counter, the tabby ducking under to hide from a bumblebee that buzzed past, and the stand’s owner—an old guy in a frayed plaid flannel, name tag that said MARTY—laughed so hard his belly shook. “Hold on, kid,” he called, wiping fryer grease on his jeans, “don’t get your cotton candy in the lard.”

I stepped up next, my boots still crunching on the leftover hay from the maze, and Marty turned to me, his face crinkling into a smile. “What can I get ya?”

I’d only come for one, I thought, just to see if it was as good as everyone said. “One, please?”

He plucked a donut out of the fryer basket, dusted it thick with honey right there at the counter—so much honey that some clumped into shiny, sticky globs on the crisp crust—and dropped it into a thin waxed paper bag. It was hot enough to burn through the paper, my fingers tingling as I wrapped them around it. “Fresh off the fryer,” he said, winking. “Don’t burn your tongue.”

I turned to leave, and the tabby darted out from under the counter right between my legs, fast as a shadow. I jumped, almost dropping the bag, and the kid yelled “SORRY!” so loud the bluegrass band paused for half a second. I laughed, holding the bag tighter, and kept walking, looking for a spot to sit.

The bench was half-hidden behind a clump of sumac, its red paint chipped so bad the gray wood showed through, splinters sticking out of the seat like tiny thorns. I sat anyway, feeling a splinter catch on the back of my jeans, and didn’t move. The creek was right in front of me, the sunset turning its surface liquid gold, a few fallen maple leaves skittering across the ripples. I opened the bag, and the steam hit my face, warm and sweet, thick with apple and cinnamon and honey.

The first bite cracked the crust so loud it made my teeth tingle, crumbs falling into my lap and onto the splintered wood. The inside was soft, almost spongy, with that sharp, bright apple cider tang that cut through the sweetness, like a bite of autumn itself. The honey was sticky on my tongue, warm enough to make my throat feel tight—not from the heat, but from how perfect it was. I’d had donuts before: store-bought, bakery-made, even homemade—but nothing like this. Nothing that tasted like a secret, like something I’d been missing my whole life without knowing.

I patted my jeans pocket out of habit, feeling the hard lump of my phone. I had a work email that was supposed to be sent that day, a text from my roommate asking if I could pick up milk on the way home, a reminder to pay my electric bill. But I didn’t take it out. I looked up, and the kid was sitting on the other side of the creek, the tabby curled up on their lap, nuzzling their neck, the half-eaten blue cotton candy resting on the rock next to them, a blue smudge on their cheek. The kid waved, and I waved back, a crumb of donut stuck to my thumb.

This perfect, bright, sticky, quiet thing that felt like it was made just for me.

Mabel’s front paws are caked in caramel so thick it glints like sap when she tilts her head, the oak’s splinters digging into her flank like tiny, uninvited audience members. The popcorn—god, the popcorn—first bite hit her tongue like a secret: sea salt sharp enough to make her whiskers twitch, caramel soft enough to melt into the fur between her toes. She’d dug it out of the downtown bodega dumpster at dusk, right when the owner locks up and the good stuff starts, and now she’s huddled under the oak like it’s a fortress, the half-eaten bag crumpled at her paws, crumbs stuck to her raccoon mask, her tail fanned out like a blanket to block the wind that carries the distant bark of a golden retriever she’d once stolen a hot dog from.

A wobbly peep, high and thin as a dandelion stem, makes her jump. Pip—she’d found him tangled in a plastic grocery bag by the playground slide three days prior, too small to fly, too loud to leave. Now he’s perched on her hind paw, his tiny claws digging into the thick gray fur, and before she can snap at him to quit, he’s snatched a crumb of popcorn, flapped his half-grown wings once, and tucked it under her tail like it’s a diamond. “Quit it,” she huffs, but her tone is soft, because she knows he’s scared of the dark, scared of the dogs that bark too loud, scared of being alone. She’d been that scared once, too, when she was a kit, stuck in a storm drain after a thunderstorm, no one to bring her crumbs, no one to tuck anything under their tail for her.

A flash of tabby fur makes her freeze. Gary. The stray with the torn left ear, the one who used to challenge her for dumpster finds by hissing so loud it rattled the trash cans, until the day he left a dead moth at her den instead of fighting. She’d thought it was a joke, at first, until he did it again: a moth with dusty wings, laid at the root of the oak like a peace offering, like he was saying I don’t want to hurt you, I just want a bite. Now he’s hiding behind the bench, the one she’d sat on last night, the one that creaks so loud it sounds like it’s crying when no one sits on it.

Oh no. Oh no no no. She’d scribbled her haiku there. She’d been writing bad, overly dramatic haikus about park benches for months, ever since the park started banning raccoons from the picnic tables, ever since she’d realized no one would sit on her bench unless she had something good to eat. Last night, when the park was empty, when she’d dragged a piece of charcoal from the smoldering grill by the picnic area, and she’d scribbled it in big, messy letters on the base of the bench, right where Gary can see it if he leans forward. It’s stupid, so stupid, the kind of thing only a sad, middle-aged raccoon would do. She’d written it after no one sat on the bench for three hours, after she’d watched a kid drop a cherry lollipop and a dog eat it, after she’d felt so lonely she’d wanted to dig a hole and stay there forever. The haiku is: Bench bleeds sap tears / No lap for my cold paws now / Only moss mourns with me. It’s terrible. Overly dramatic. So embarrassing. She’d never let anyone see it, not even Pip, who’d only ever seen her eat half a tuna can and fall asleep on a trash can lid.

Gary steps out from behind the bench, slow, like he’s scared she’ll run. He drops a moth at the oak’s root, same as always, and Mabel’s heart does a stupid little flip. He’s not here to fight. He’s here to ask for popcorn. In his weird, moth-shaped way.

Pip steals another crumb, tucks it under his own wing this time, and Mabel sighs. She nudges a crumb toward the moth, toward Gary, and he blinks, slow, like he’s surprised. The oak creaks, the caramel is sticky on her paws, Pip is peeping so loud it makes her ears hurt, and Gary is staring at the bench, at the haiku, and Mabel is ready to bolt, ready to dig a hole and hide forever, until Gary tilts his head, and she swears she sees a tiny, cat-like smile. Maybe he doesn’t care about the haiku. Maybe he just likes the popcorn. Maybe he’s lonely, too. Maybe all of them are, in their own weird, messy, wonderful ways. (Word count: 709)

The crumbs were all gone. The pigeon had hogged the last hot dog bit, and the birdseed in the feeder was stale, the kind that makes my throat itch. I hopped under the oak bench to get away from the pigeon’s strutting, my scruffy brown feathers sticking up where the blueberry tuft from last summer’s muffin still wouldn’t wash out, and that’s when I saw it.

Bright blue, crinkly, soft plastic, with little cartoon kids grinning on the side. It smelled like sugar and something sharp, like the lemon off the playground tree but ten times stronger. I pecked at it once, twice, and it gave a little. I was already chirping, quiet, so the pigeon wouldn’t hear, when the shadow fell.

Chitter. Loud, sharp, the kind that makes my ears ring. It was Nutty, the squirrel that stole my sunflower seed stash last winter, the one with the white patch on his tail. He lunged for the bag, his paws out, and I panicked. My tail puffed up so much I could barely see over it, my wings fluttered so hard I kicked up dirt that got in my eyes, and I pecked his front paw as hard as I could—hard enough that I felt my beak ache. He yelped, dropped the acorn he was holding, and scurried back, his tail flicking. I grabbed the bag with my beak, yanking so hard my neck hurt, and flew up to the low fence, landing so hard I slid a little.

I dropped the bag on the rail and pecked a hole in the plastic. The sugar dust on the outside—from the kid’s sticky hand, I bet—got all over my claws. I tried to grip the rail to steady myself, and my claws stuck. I yanked them off so fast a tuft of my scruffy wing feather, the one with the blueberry stain, got stuck to the plastic. I pulled out a red Sour Patch, and the sugar on the candy stuck more. I tried to preen my claw, and my beak stuck. I wiped it on the rail, and sugar came off in little clumps, but my claws were still sticky, leaving tiny brown prints on the gray wood when I hopped.

I bit the red one first. Sweet, a little sour, boring. I spit it out. The yellow one was better, more sour, but still not enough. Then I pulled out a green one.

The sour hit me so hard my eyes watered. My beak twitched so hard I dropped the candy for a second, then grabbed it again before it could roll off the rail. It was sharp, bright, like the first bite of a lemon but better, like something that made my whole chest feel tingly. I looked into the bag, and that’s when I saw them—piled under the red and yellow ones, a whole stack of green Sour Patch Kids, all for me.

My heart started beating so fast I could feel it in my chest. I chirped so loud the sparrow on the next fence flinched. I hopped up and down so much I almost fell off the rail. I thought of my secret nest, the hollow in the gutter of the old library, too high for squirrels, too narrow for pigeons, no one knew about it. I could carry each green one one by one, hide them, eat them all by myself, no sharing, no Nutty stealing them, no pigeons hogging them.

The giddy feeling was better than the blueberry muffin. Better than the sunflower seeds I found last spring. It was like flying on a warm wind, like finding a whole patch of dandelion fluff to roll in, but all mine. All the green ones. All the sour ones.

Wake up first thing, always, the lavender hits me before my eyes even open—soft, like the librarian’s soap, like the way the sun feels on my back when I’m perched on the chipped blue saucer. The nest is poetry pages, thin and crinkly, and I can feel the edge of a word under my wing, something like “home” maybe? I can’t read, but it feels like a hug. Then the first sound is the record player, soft scratchy through the floorboards, like the librarian is humming right into my bones, off-key sometimes, but that’s the best part, like she’s not trying to be perfect, just being her.

I stretch, and my belly is all round, from the crumb I saved last night—sourdough crust, chewy, the kind that’s so hard I have to peck at it three times before it breaks, and when it does, it’s warm, like it was just taken out of the oven even though it’s been on the saucer all day. The saucer has little white flowers, and sometimes the librarian leaves a sunflower seed right in the middle, shiny and hard, and I can crack it open with my beak, and the inside is soft and salty, better than any bug I’ve ever chased. Sometimes she leaves a crumb with a little smudge of jam on it by accident, sticky sweet, and I lick it off slow, my feathers getting all messy, and I don’t even care. The sourdough crumbs sometimes have a little bit of salt on them, from her baking, and it makes them taste even better, like the sea even though we’re miles from it.

Then if the window’s open—oh, the window, the one that’s always a little stuck, so the librarian has to push it hard to close it, and sometimes she forgets, and that’s the best day of the week. When it’s open, the pine from the woods hits me first, sharp and green, and then the clover, sweet, like honey, and the woodpecker tapping on the oak, loud and fast, and I tap back, just for fun, even though he never answers, but it feels like we’re talking.

I fly out, and the wind is soft, like a hand on my feathers, and sometimes I catch a dandelion fluff, and it sticks to my wing for a second, white and light, before blowing away. The clover patch is all green and white, little flowers everywhere, and I hop around, and there are snails with shiny shells, and bumblebees that look like little moving clouds, fuzzy and slow, and they buzz past my ear, and it’s warm, like a hug. Sometimes I pick a clover flower, hold it in my beak for a second, sweet and soft, before dropping it, and it falls slow, like a little gift. The other sparrows come around sometimes, chirp loud, tease me for being too chubby to fly fast, but I just peck at a crumb and chirp back, because what do they have? They have bugs and grass seeds, I have sourdough crust and lavender nest and the librarian’s off-key singing.

I fly back, and the attic is all gold when the sun is low, the dust motes glowing like tiny embers, and I flap my wings, and they swirl around my head, like confetti, and I chirp, just because it feels good. When the sun is really bright, the dust motes look like tiny stars, and I flap my wings to make them swirl, and it feels like I’m flying through the sky even when I’m in the attic. I perch on the rafter that has a little bit of moss growing on it, soft and green, and rest my feet there, and watch the dust. Sometimes the librarian comes up to get a blanket, and she talks to me, “Hi Pip, you’re being a little piggy with the crumbs again,” and it’s soft, not mean, like she’s glad I’m there.

When it rains, the window is closed, and the rain hits the roof, soft and loud, like a lullaby, and the librarian makes tea, cinnamon tea, and the steam comes up through the floorboards, and it smells like Christmas, even in July. I burrow into the nest, into the lavender lint, and I can hear the TV playing soft, and the record player, and it’s all warm, like I’m wrapped up in a blanket of sound. Sometimes I drink rainwater from the cracked teacup in the corner, the one with the chip on the rim, and the water tastes like pine and rain, cool and sweet. The first thing I feel when I step out from under the rotting boardwalk where I hid during the storm is the weight of my fur. It’s not soaked through— I’d tucked my head under my belly when the rain lashed sideways, so only the tuft of white on my chest and the tips of my tabby stripes are damp, cold enough to make the nick in my left ear tingle when the wind stirs. The wind is soft now, not the howl that made the boardwalk creak like it would snap, and the quiet is thick, layered: drip, drip, drip from the gutters strung between the firs, the distant, lazy crash of waves that’s lost its angry edge, the soft squelch of moss under my calloused paw pads when I step off the concrete.

Smell hits me next, sharp and sweet and briny all at once. Brine from the Strait, thick enough to taste on my tongue, mixed with the pine tang of the old-growth firs that line the edge of town, the damp loam of the flower beds where marigolds are still half-blooming, a faint tang of diesel from the fishing boat tied up at the dock, and then—warm. Cinnamon, sugar, butter, vanilla, so bright it cuts through the brine like a fish through water.

I veer off the main street, my paws leaving soft, dark prints on the wet asphalt, and follow the smell to the chipped blue cottage on the corner. Its porch step is half-rotted but dry enough, and the half-eaten cinnamon roll sits right on the edge, glaze still tacky, crumbs scattered like tiny stars. I climb the step slow, my dull claws clicking on the wood, and sniff it first— the warm sugar makes my nose twitch, the cinnamon is sharp enough to make my eyes water a little. I take a bite, soft dough that gives under my teeth, sweet glaze that sticks to my scruffy chin, a crunch of cinnamon sugar on the edge that makes my whiskers vibrate. I lick the crumbs off my chin, the taste lingering, warm and sweet, long after I step off the porch.

That’s when the sun breaks through.

I stop mid-step, my paws on the asphalt, and the light hits me. It’s low, late October sun, pink and golden, and it turns the wet asphalt the color of the inside of a pink seashell, glowing soft and bright. The cold water on my paw pads warms just a little, enough to make me wiggle my toes, and the light makes my tabby stripes glow orange, bright as a campfire. I blink, squint, the sun is bright enough to make the world go white at the edges for a second, and I tilt my head up, the light hitting my face, warm on the nick in my ear, warm on the damp tuft of my chest.

The sun only stays for a minute, just long enough for me to turn in a circle on the pink asphalt, and then it’s gone, hidden behind gray clouds again, the pink fading to dark gray. I wander down the alley between the blue cottage and the next one, lined with blackberry bushes heavy with dark, damp berries. I brush against a bush, a berry falls right at my paws, and I sniff it— sweet and tart, a little earthy. I lick it off my paw, the juice staining my fur purple for a second, and then I dig in the pile of cedar shavings left by the roof repair crew, kicking up a cloud of dust that glows pink for a second before it settles.

When I wander out of the alley, the cottages are closer to the ocean, the air a little sharper, and I see it: the cottage with the fairy lights, strung along the porch, little warm white ones glowing through the gray. I hear the song before I see it, soft, a guitar strumming, a woman’s voice low, humming, like she’s singing to herself. It hums in my chest, soft and warm, like the purr of a big cat I met once, when I was a kitten, under the boardwalk.

I climb up to the porch, it’s raised a foot off the ground, and I squeeze into the gap under it, between the porch floor and the soft, dry dirt. It’s tight, just enough for me to curl up, my scruffy fur brushing the wood above me, and the dirt is warm— the sun hit the porch floor earlier, radiating down, warm enough to seep into my belly, to dry the damp tuft on my chest.

I curl up, tucking my paws under my chin, and watch the fairy lights glow through the gaps in the porch floor, little spots of warm light on my fur. I can hear the drip of rain from the porch edge, the soft crash of waves, the song humming in my chest. No one is calling me, no one is chasing me, no one is leaving food out for me to beg for, no one is wanting anything from me. I don’t have to hunt, don’t have to hide, don’t have to run.

The afternoon stretches, slow and soft, and I blink, the warm light on my face, the taste of cinnamon and blackberry on my tongue, the sound of the song and the waves and the drip of rain, and for a second, I forget about the raccoon that nicked my ear, about the cold nights when I have to hide under the boardwalk, about the way the rain lashed sideways during the storm. I’m just Mochi, scruffy tabby, warm under the porch, the world quiet and soft and mine, for as long as the afternoon lasts.

The bookstore doesn’t show up on any maps, not even the hand-drawn ones I’ve stitched into the lining of my coat for chasing weird books. I’d been tramping through the rain for three hours, chasing a 1912 copy of *The Mouse Who Ate Socks* that a bookseller in Portland had sworn existed, when I turned a corner off a cracked sidewalk and suddenly the air smelled like old lavender, faint mildew, and burnt toffee. I blinked, and there it was: a two-story wooden building with leaded glass windows, one of which had a crack shaped like a lopsided sock, sun slanting through the glass so it made gold splotches on the warped floorboards inside. The sign above the door was hand-painted, peeling, and said *Mabel’s Book Nook* – not the usual name for a sock-eating mouse book shop, but I didn’t hesitate. I turned the brass doorknob, which was shaped like a tiny sock, and stepped inside.

I’d been inside for maybe two minutes, tracing the gold splotches on the floor, when I saw it: a nook tucked between a shelf of 1910s penny dreadfuls and a stack of 1930s zines titled *Sock Fanciers Quarterly*, locked with a brass padlock shaped like a sock. The padlock had a tiny scratch on its side that looked like a cat’s paw print. I’d been carrying a keychain for three months, a tiny fabric sock doll I’d bought at a flea market in Ohio, its white paw and orange tail frayed from being jangled in my pocket. I pressed the doll’s paw to the padlock, and it clicked open.

I reached in, and my fingers closed around something tiny, palm-sized, warm from the sun that had been hitting the nook. It was the only copy of *Mabel’s Lost Sock Adventures*, the title printed in faded gold on an indigo cover, embossed with a lopsided sock that had a tiny, sad face – like a kid had drawn it, not a professional illustrator. The edges of the cover were frayed, so soft they felt like moth wings when I brushed them.

I flipped to the first page, and there was Mabel, a girl with braids tied with red ribbon, chasing her sock through a garden of dandelion fluff. The next page had a dark purple stain, seeped through from the front, the color of the grape popsicle I’d eaten every Saturday when I was seven. It was on page 3, right where Mabel’s sock was running off into the dandelions. I ran my thumb over the stain, and it felt like paper that had been pressed flat after being wet, like Lila, the kid who owned this book, had spilled her grape juice on it while reading.

I flipped slowly, each page sticking a little to my thumb, until I got to page 12. The illustration there was Mabel sitting on a windowsill, her sock in her hand, the same red ribbon tied around the sock’s ankle. Right on the sock’s toe, there was a faint, smudged fingerprint, so small it could only have been a seven-year-old’s thumb. I pulled my phone out to check the time, and the screen was dead – the bookstore always drains the battery of people who don’t belong, or maybe it was just the rain. I didn’t care. I’d been inside for seven minutes, and it felt like I’d been there for hours, like the sun had slowed down just to let me look. I pressed my own thumb next to the print, and for a second it felt like I was pressing against Lila’s hand, like she was right there, sitting next to me, her sticky grape juice fingers still warm. Under the illustration, in faded pencil, was scrawled: *Tangerine is my best friend*, next to a lopsided drawing of a cat – orange, with a white paw, a tiny triangular face that looked like it was grinning.

I was leaning in to trace the cat’s face when something small and sticky fell out of the book’s spine, clattering onto the floor. I picked it up, and it was a half-eaten lemon drop, so old the sugar had crystallized into tiny sharp points, crusted with fine book dust, the bite mark on it tiny, curved, like a cat’s tooth. It had probably been there since 1927, when Lila was seven, reading this book in her bedroom, sneaking candy while her mom wasn’t looking. I sniffed it, and it smelled like lemon and old lavender, the same sachets I’d seen tucked into the spines of the shelves, stitched with tiny sock faces. I wiped a little of the dust off on my coat and tucked it into my pocket, where it would sit next to the crumpled receipt for the 1912 mouse book I’d never found.

Just then, a jingle drifted through the cracked back window, slow and warped, like the speaker was dying. It was *Pop Goes the Weasel*, the same song my mom used to sing to me when I lost my socks. I looked up, and through the window I could see the ice cream truck, painted pale blue, with a sign on the side that said *Sock Shaped Popsicles* in lopsided letters. It was idling at the curb, the driver leaning out to talk to the man in the café cart outside, the one selling burnt toffee. I stood there for a minute, listening to the jingle, thinking about going out to buy a popsicle, but the book in my hand was too warm, too soft, so I stayed.

That’s when I noticed him. He was sitting in a chair by the back window, the sun hitting his silver hair so it looked like spun sugar, wearing a gray wool sweater with a hole at the elbow, covered in orange and white cat hair. He was holding a tattered copy of *Sock Witches of the Hudson Valley*, a book I’d been looking for for two years, and he’d been watching me. I felt his eyes on me, so I held up the book, flipped to the inside back cover, and showed him the map.

The map was tiny, drawn in pencil, crinkled at the edges, like Lila had folded it up a hundred times. It showed the bookstore’s layout: the front door, the penny dreadful shelf, the back window, and an X marked right next to the shelf of 1920s board games, under a tiny note that said *Tangerine’s Spot*. I traced the X with my finger, and the man nodded.

His smile was tiny, knowing, like he’d seen this map a hundred times, like he’d been looking for this book for years. He held up his own keychain, and it was a tiny fabric sock doll, just like mine, with a white paw and an orange tail, frayed at the edges. He didn’t say anything, just nodded again, and I knew. He was Lila’s grandson. Lila had hidden the book here, years ago, and he’d been coming to the bookstore, looking for it, just like I’d been coming, looking for weird books.

I flipped back to page 15, and there was another margin, scrawled in the same pencil: *Tangerine found my sock under the porch*, next to a tiny drawing of a porch with a cat peeking out. I ran my thumb over the words, and the book stuck a little to my skin, like it didn’t want me to leave. The ice cream truck jingle faded, and the man turned back to his book, the cat hair on his sweater shifting when he moved. I put *Mabel’s Lost Sock Adventures* back in the nook, locked it with the brass sock padlock, and the sun hit the nook just right, making the book’s indigo cover glow for a second, like it was waving goodbye.

I turned to leave, the doorknob cold when I touched it, but the lemon drop in my pocket was still warm, and I knew I’d be back. The bookstore only appears when you’re looking for something weird, something that matters, and I was already thinking about what I’d chase next.

My official job is to nap on the front desk, so I curl back up, but the stack of *Caterpillar*s is lumpy now, so I nudge a regular library copy of *Where the Wild Things Are* open to the wolf-suit page and lay my head on that. The rain seeps in the door crack, and I hate wet paws, so I stay put until the first patron comes in: a 2nd grader with sparkly pink rain boots, holding a drawing of a T-Rex. Clara lets her pick a dinosaur book, and I doze for ten minutes until I hear the back door jingle—teens, the early release ones: Mia, Javi, Leo, hiding in the graphic novel nook.

That’s my first unofficial duty: trip them for sour straws. I slip off the desk when Clara’s busy checking in a box of donated Mary Oliver poetry books, weave through the stacks, my paws silent on linoleum, until I’m behind the shelves of tattered old Harlequin paperbacks. Javi is kneeling, reaching for a pack of blue sour straws in his backpack, and I step on his shoelace on purpose. He yelps so loud a shelf of Archie comics rattles, and the whole pack spills. I pounce on the blue ones first, chew one so hard my whiskers get sticky with sugar. Mia laughs, says “Mochi, you’re the worst,” and shoves a cherry one at me. I eat it while Javi ties his shoe, then nip Leo’s ankle playfully when he tries to grab a stray blue one. He yelps too. Perfect.

Wednesday is my book-stealing day. The new releases cart is shiny, full of books wrapped in plastic, but I don’t want those. I climb the cart, claws catching on plastic, and knock over a stack of picture books—*Goodnight Moon* falls open to the moon page, and I nudge it with my paw before spotting the tiny, beat-up paperback of *The Little Prince* someone donated last night: no plastic wrap, cover scuffed, spine cracked. I tuck it under my chin, run as fast as I can to the heating vent behind the mystery section, and hide it under a loose floorboard. Then I sprint back to the desk, like I was napping the whole time.

That’s when the door jingles again. The rain is so hard now it sounds like rocks hitting the skylight. In comes the stranger: neon lime raincoat so bright it hurts my eyes, hood up so I can’t see their face, holding a jar of glowing fireflies. The fireflies glow so bright they light up the linoleum. They walk up to the desk, pull a water-stained 1972 copy of *Where the Wild Things Are* out of their raincoat pocket, and tuck it under Clara’s nose. “I want to check this out,” they say, their voice rough, like they’ve been yelling in the wind. Clara leans in, gasps. The bookmark is a pressed green sea glass, shaped like a little fish, tucked between the pages where Max dances with the Wild Things. “That’s the copy from the 1998 storm,” Clara says. “When the basement flooded. I thought it was lost forever.” The stranger pulls out a crumpled photo: a little girl with pigtails, holding a tabby cat that looks just like me, standing on the beach. Clara’s eyes fill with tears.

The stranger pays with a crumpled $5 bill, puts the *Wild Things* back in their raincoat, and leaves. A gust of wind blows the door open right after, and rain splashes all over my white sock paw. I yelp, hide under the desk for a minute, then remember: they forgot the firefly jar. It’s sitting right next to my sticky paw. I sniff it: wet grass, pine, the cove down by the lighthouse, the beach where that photo was taken. I grab it in my mouth—light, so light, like carrying a tiny sun—and Clara laughs while she slams the door shut. “Mochi, you’re so dramatic,” she says.

Then the poetry club comes in: elderly ladies with their Mary Oliver books. Clara is setting up folding chairs, and she starts crying hard, the kind where her shoulders shake. That’s my third unofficial duty: console her. I jump up on her lap, nudge her hand with my head, and knock over her copy of *Devotions* so it falls open to the “Wild Geese” page. She laughs, wipes her tears on her sleeve, and says “You’re such a good cat, Mochi.”

The teens come back from lunch and left a whole pack of sour straws on the desk just for me. I eat so many my stomach hurts, then I knock over Clara’s lemon tea, which spills all over the poetry club’s tablecloth. The ladies laugh, say “Mochi, you’re a scamp,” and give me a sugar cookie with sprinkles. I hide half of it under the desk for later.

At 5pm, Clara locks the door, turns off all the lights except the skylight and the little lamp by the heating vent. I run to the loose floorboard behind the mystery section, grab my stolen *The Little Prince*, then run back to the desk to get the firefly jar. I carry the jar in my mouth and the book under my other paw, and I run to the vent.

The vent is so warm it makes my fur feel soft, smells like old paper and dust and rain. I curl up, lay the *Little Prince* on my chest, the firefly jar next to me. The fireflies glow so bright the pages light up, and I can see the fox, the rose, the little prince’s hair even in the dark. The rain is still drumming on the skylight, soft again, like someone tapping my head with a wet paw, and I hear Clara humming from the front desk—the same song she hums when she’s happy.

I lick the last of the sugar off my whiskers, and I’m sticky, and my stomach hurts a little, and my paw is still a little honey-sticky, and it’s perfect.

The secret third floor is only accessible if you bring the forgotten thing: a pressed four-leaf clover, the kind that grows only in the overgrown vacant lot behind the store, blooming exclusively on October 12—Mabel’s opening day. On that first day in 1923, Mabel tucked one of these clovers into the back of every book she sold, telling each customer, “This is for the thing you haven’t found yet.” No one remembered that line; for decades, the clovers sat forgotten between the pages of *The Waste Land*, *Little Women*, lurid dime novels about gangsters, until someone would dig one out of an attic box, squint at it, and suddenly recall Mabel’s voice, soft and bright, and bring it to the front desk.

When you tap the spine of *The Great Gatsby* three times with the clover in your hand, a false shelf of 1920s dime novels swings open to reveal oak stairs worn smooth by 100 years of feet, each step creaking in the exact rhythm of the first line of *The Waste Land*: April is the cruellest month. The air hits you first: layered scents of melted beeswax (hand-dipped candles, wicks trimmed every night), rain on cedar window frames, lavender sachets tucked into every book spine, and the faint, sweet fizz of root beer floats from a 1920s soda fountain tucked into the back corner.

The third floor is wonky, expanded three times over the decades, so it’s full of nooks that feel like secrets:
- The Nook of Unsent Letters: floor-to-ceiling reclaimed barn wood shelves stacked with sealed envelopes, waxed red, purple, gold, addressed to dead lovers, childhood friends, the version of yourself you were 10 years prior. A faded blue velvet armchair with a frayed crocheted blanket sits by a glass-shaded lamp painted with roses, casting warm orange light that makes the envelopes glow like embers.
- The Nook of Half-Finished Stories: shelves lined with notebooks—leather-bound, spiral, plain paper held together with rubber bands—each holding a half-written plot, a single first sentence, a napkin scrawled with a character’s name. A 1920s Underwood typewriter sits on a small oak desk, its keys worn smooth, typing whatever you think, no typos, no mistakes.
- The Nook of Forgotten Dreams: glass shelves holding objects that never got to be: a pink ballet slipper with a broken toe, name scrawled on the sole; a half-finished oil painting of a Hudson sunset, sky painted in oranges so bright they look like they’re burning; a baseball glove with “Tom” carved into the leather; a pilot’s license never used, the photo of a young man grinning like he’s about to fly. A 1920s Victrola plays only the songs that were never recorded, the ones bands played once at a party, the ones people forgot the words to.

The floorboards are scuffed, and if you kneel to look closely, you can see initials carved into the oak with pocket knives: M + J 1923 (Mabel and her girlfriend, who died in the 1927 flu), L 1956 (a kid who came in with a clover after his dad left), E 2001 (a teen who showed up after 9/11, looking for something to hold onto). At the end of the hall, a leaded glass bay window looks out over a park that doesn’t exist anymore: Central Park in 1923, flappers in drop-waist dresses, men in straw boaters playing croquet, a jazz band playing soft in the distance.

If you stay past 10pm on a rainy Tuesday, the brass bell on the front desk rings once, soft as a secret. The beeswax candles gutter, then brighten, casting long dancing shadows that look like suffragists and flappers and kids chasing fireflies. The root beer taps hiss, and a float appears on the counter in front of you, vanilla ice cream melting just slow enough to taste the fizz under the sweetness. Mabel leans against the bay window, which is now open, rain falling in slow perfect arcs that don’t touch the floor, the books, or you. Her bob is still neat, her purple and gold suffrage sash still bright, her boots scuffed from walking the store’s nooks for 100 years. “I stayed once,” she says. “Rainy Tuesday, 1923. I’d just sold my first copy of *The Waste Land* to a poet scared to publish his work, and I forgot to lock up.”

The shelves start to hum, a low warm sound like all the books breathing. The half-finished story you wrote in 2019 about the girl who could talk to cats is now a finished book on the Underwood’s shelf, your name on the spine, pages filled with the words you never got to write. The ballet slipper you bought at 12, thrown in the back of your closet after your mom got sick, is now on your feet, soft and perfect, and you can dance even though you haven’t danced in years, even though you thought you’d forgotten how. The version of you that you would have been—if you’d gone to art school, if you’d told your best friend you loved them, if you’d kept writing that story, if you’d kept dancing—steps out from behind the shelf of unsent letters. They look like you, but happier, their hair a little longer, their smile a little brighter, and they hand you a pressed four-leaf clover, just like the one you brought. “I’ve been waiting for you,” they say.

You have a choice: stay, and live that life—the one you forgot, the one you were scared to want—or go back, and take a piece of it with you: the finished book, the memory of dancing, the courage to tell someone you love them, the clover that will let you come back anytime. If you go back, the clover you brought becomes a permanent part of you, so you can return, again and again, whenever you need the thing you haven’t found yet.

Then wood smoke—sweet oak, a hint of pine, curling from the cast-iron stove in the center of the store, crackling so loud it makes the air hum, low and thrumming, like the store itself is breathing.

I hang my coat on a peg shaped like a hermit crab, the brass cold under my fingers, and notice the poetry nook first. It’s a cranny built into the wall, lined with frayed velvet cushions, a coffee stain blotted into the gray fabric, and the teen is camped there, just as described. They’re wearing a faded gray hoodie with a blue whale on the back, their hair half-up, a strand of seaweed stuck to the end of a braid, scribbling in a leather notebook with a fountain pen. Their thermos is chipped blue, a faded orange fox sticker stuck to the side, and they don’t look up when I step in—just keep scribbling, the pen’s scratch soft, almost lost under the stove’s crackle.

The store is tiny, shelves stacked to the ceiling, leaning a little, some with chipped cream paint, cluttered with loose books, a brass sextant, a stack of fishing logs from 1952, a pressed sea lavender tucked between the pages of *The Little Prince*. I wander slow, no rush, no plan, my fingers brushing spines: a 1968 *Charlotte’s Web* with a cracked spine, a copy of *Moby Dick* bound in black leather, a stack of local coastal poetry. When I reach the shelf of children’s books, my fingers catch on a book tucked between *Moby Dick* and *Charlotte’s Web*—a 1972 *The Hobbit*, its spine cracked in three places, the cover faded to a soft brown, the original illustration of Bilbo’s hobbit hole chipped where someone’s held it a hundred times.

I pick it up, and the first thing I notice is the warmth—its spine is hot from being near the stove, the paper thin and yellowed, soft under my fingers. I carry it to the poetry nook, sink into the velvet cushion next to the teen, and when I shift to make room, my elbow knocks a stack of Mary Oliver books, and a dented blue tin tumbles out, tucked behind the stack, half-hidden by a frayed throw. It’s the same blue as the teen’s thermos, the same orange fox sticker stuck to the lid, and when I lift it, the smell hits me—bright lemon, rich butter, a hint of sea salt, warm, so warm the metal is hot under my fingers. I pop the lid, and there are six pieces left, crumbs at the bottom, a little grease stain on the lid from where someone held it.

I flip open the Hobbit, and the marginalia jumps out first—blue ballpoint, smudged in places, like the writer cried while writing, or spilled soda on the page. The first note is on page 47, next to the part where Bilbo meets Gollum: “he’s scared too, just like me”. Then page 122, next to the battle of the five armies: “don’t be brave if it hurts”. And then page 147, the part I know is her favorite—when Bilbo sits by the fire with the dwarves after the battle, when they laugh and eat and stop being scared for a minute. The note there is written in bigger letters, smudged at the edges, like she wrote it fast, excited: “this is what it feels like when you finally stop being scared enough to eat cookies and laugh”. And next to it, a tiny fox, thumb-sized, curled up by a tiny fire, an acorn at its paws. On the next page, another fox, holding a piece of shortbread, and the words: “shortbread is better than treasure”.

I laugh soft, so soft it’s almost lost under the stove’s crackle, and the teen glances up for half a second—their eyes are gray, like the mist outside, and they nod, just a small, quick nod, before going back to scribbling. I hold the Hobbit up to my ear, and I can hear it—the hum, the thrumming, the stove’s vibration traveling through the paper, making the pages sing low, like a secret. The rain is tapping the leaded windows now, soft knocks, sometimes a gust of wind makes the glass rattle, and the stove pops so loud it makes me jump a little, the hum rising for a second before settling back.

I take a piece of shortbread from the tin, and it crumbles when I pick it up, a crumb falling on page 147, right next to Lila’s fox. I brush it off slow, no rush, and take a bite. It’s warm, the lemon zing bright, the salt cutting the sweetness, the butter rich, melting on my tongue. I sit there for a long time, flipping through the Hobbit, tracing Lila’s foxes with my finger, reading her notes, feeling the hum of the pages under my hand. The teen’s pen scratches soft, the stove crackles, the rain taps, the waves rumble distant and muffled by the mist.

I don’t check my phone. I don’t think about the grocery list I left on the counter, or the text I need to send my mom, or the meeting I have tomorrow. No one needs me for these three hours—no one is waiting, no one is asking, no one is expecting anything. The light is soft gray, mid-November, the stove casting orange streaks across the shelves, half the store in shadow, half in warm light. I eat another piece of shortbread, crumbs falling on my coat, and flip to the end of the book, where Lila wrote: “I hope I find my fire someday”.

When the three hours are almost up, I don’t want to leave. The mist is still thick outside, the rain still tapping, the stove still crackling, the pages still humming. The teen puts down their pen, stretches, and grabs the tin of shortbread, takes a piece, and I do too. We don’t say anything. We just sit there, eating shortbread, listening to the rain, feeling the hum of the store, and for a minute, it feels like I found Lila’s fire too.

The draft nips my ear tips, so I tuck my head into my chest, fluffing my fur until I’m a round, warm ball. The panes are wavy, so the rain looks like falling silver threads, the oak outside looks like a blurry green monster, the sky looks like a gray blanket someone left out to dry.

I jump down, soft, the velvet armrest of the oak chair catching my paws first—scratched up by a girl who cried here last week, her hair stuck to her cheek when she left, so I rub my cheek on the scratch to say hello to her ghost. When I step onto the left page, it crinkles soft, so soft only I can hear it, like stepping on dried rose petals. The paper is yellowed, ink faded blue, so the words look like smudged stars. The sachets are little, faded, some with tiny embroidered roses, some plain linen, tucked between the spines of cracked leather and frayed cloth and yellowed paper that smells like old secrets. I rub my cheek on a plain linen sachet, and the lavender sticks to my fur, so when I walk, I leave a soft lavender trail across the floor, like I’m marking my territory even though no one else cares.

Now the secret. It’s tiny, just for me, something no one else knows. Behind the third shelf on the west wall, the one with all the poetry books, there’s a gap in the wall just big enough for me to squeeze through—no one else is small enough to fit. Inside, there’s a patch of moss that glows soft green, only when I’m there, and it’s my space. I keep little things there: a tiny mother-of-pearl button a boy left when he remembered how to stop and watch the rain, a crumpled daisy petal the girl with the hair stuck to her cheek left, a half-written note that says “thank you” that I found tucked in a book. The rain starts on Monday, soft at first, then hard, thudding on the slate roof like someone tapping my rim with a spoon, only slower, deeper. I’m thin, bone china, 1927, made in Stoke-on-Trent, the lady of the house bought me for her sister’s wedding tea party, the roses on my side are faded pink, almost gray, and my rim has a chip—jagged, half an inch long, on the left side, I always get that wrong, it’s not the right, it’s the left—from when Mrs. Hale tripped over a loose floorboard in 1952, carrying me up to the attic after the lady died. She cried, I remember that, her hands were rough from scrubbing floors but soft when she wrapped me in the tea towel that still smells like earl grey, even after all these years. The lady used to put a little lemon in the tea, right? Thin slices, so the juice seeped through the china, sweet and sharp, I can almost taste it when the wind blows through the attic.

I’m in a cardboard box under the eaves, next to a moth-eaten wool blanket that smells like the lady’s husband, who wore it when he went hunting, next to a broken tin toy soldier with a dent in his helmet, next to a half-finished cross-stitch of a rose—same pattern as mine, weird, right?—next to a box of love letters tied with frayed blue ribbon, no one has read them since 1946. The box has a sticker on it, “MRS. HALE’S THINGS” in faded blue ink, peeling at the edges, I can feel it through the cardboard when the box shifts, rough, like sandpaper.

The spider comes on Monday afternoon, small, brown—not black, I know I said brown, right?—crawls up my handle, her legs are little prickles, not bad, just there. She spins her web between my handle and the edge of the box, cool silk, sticky, and I can feel her when she crawls across it, little shifts, like a breath on my side. She talks in clicks, soft, like the rain on the roof, and she tells me about the flies that get stuck, how she likes the rain because it makes the web glisten, how she’s going to lay her eggs soon. Wait, no, she said that on Tuesday? No, Monday, I think. The rain makes time blur, like the faded roses on my side.

The other objects have secrets, silly, unimportant, the kind no one cares about but us. The toy soldier—his arm is off, he’s been lying on the floor next to the box since 1978, when a boy dropped him while playing soldiers—his secret is that he thought the Queen was coming to visit the cottage, so he hid in the toy box to spy, but then the boy dropped him, and he’s been stuck ever since, embarrassed he never got to report that the Queen never came, that he never got to be a real spy. The cross-stitch, she’s half done, the rose is only three petals, and her secret is that she started it for the lady, who loved roses, but she got bored halfway through, so she’s pretending she’s scared to be finished—scared someone will take her down and hang her in the sitting room, where the sun will fade her even more—but really she just likes being next to the photo album that has a picture of the lady holding me, the day I was new, her pearl ring glinting in the sun. The love letters, they’re from a girl named Elsie to a boy named Tom, who went to the war and never came back, and her secret is that she never sent them, she was scared Tom would think she was too silly, too soft, and now she writes little addendums to them in the margins, like “the roses by the gate bloomed pink this year” “a spider lives on the fence, spins pretty webs” “it rained all week in October”, even though no one will ever read them, even though Tom is gone.

On Tuesday, it rains so hard that the slate roof leaks a little, a drop of water falls on the spider’s web, makes it glisten like a little jewel, and the spider clicks soft, happy, and the drop rolls down my rim, cool, wet, and I can feel it through the bone china, all the way to my base. The wind blows through the cracked attic window, makes the love letters rustle, makes the cross-stitch flutter, makes the toy soldier roll a little, and I can feel the wind through the cardboard, through the tea towel, through my bone, cold but nice, like the lady’s hand when she held me for the first time.

On Wednesday, the spider crawls into my chip, the jagged hollow, and I can feel her little body press against the edge, warm, and she clicks, says she’s going to lay her eggs there. I’m happy about that, more happy than I’ve been in a long time. The chip is mine, right? It’s not a flaw, it’s part of me, like the faded roses, like the earl grey smell of the tea towel.

Then the kid comes on Thursday. I hear her before I see her, the creak of the attic ladder, the thud of her wellies on the floor, the sniffling of a cold. She’s looking for her teddy bear, the one with the missing eye, under the blanket next to my box. She trips over the toy soldier, who is lying on the floor, and knocks my box over. The lid comes off, I roll a little, the chip catches on the edge of the box, and I can feel the cardboard scrape against the jagged edge, little sharp pricks, and the sticker comes off a little, rough, scraping my base. She picks me up, her hand is warm, soft, with a little callus on her thumb from climbing trees, and she rubs the chip with her thumb, says “oh, pretty cup” and I can feel her breath on my rim, warm, smelling like peppermint. Then her mom calls, loud, from downstairs: “Lila! Come down for hot cocoa!” and she puts me back in the box, shoves it under the eaves, and leaves. I’m scared for a minute, that she’ll take me, that I’ll be put on a shelf in the sitting room, or used for tea again, but she doesn’t. She leaves me, and the spider is still on my handle, and the chip is still there, and I’m relieved.

On Friday, the spider lays her eggs in my chip. I can feel them, little soft lumps, warm, and she clicks soft, says they’ll hatch in the spring, little spiders, and I’ll have company. That makes me happy, more happy than I’ve been in a long time.

On Saturday, the rain stops for a little while, and the sun comes out, pink and gold, and hits my pattern, makes the faded roses look bright again, like they did when I was new, and the cross-stitch says “oh, you look like you did when you were new” and I remember the lady holding me, the tea party, the earl grey tea, the lady’s sister laughing, the pearl ring glinting in the sun.

On Sunday, the rain starts again, soft, and I listen to the other objects’ secrets, the spider clicks, the love letters rustle, the toy soldier rolls a little, and I feel the eggs in my chip, warm, soft, and I’m happy. I don’t want to be found. I don’t want to be put on a shelf, or used for tea, or taken down from the attic. I’m happy here, under the eaves, with the rain, the spider, the other objects, the chip that’s mine, the memory of Mrs. Hale’s hand, the memory of the lady holding me. This is perfect. Wait, is it? Yeah, it is. No one will ever find me, and that’s exactly what I want.

I’ve lived here 11 years, long enough to know the smell of lemon Pledge and old paper and the way the custodian’s vacuum sounds like a giant bee when it rumbles down the hall.

First, the goldfish. That was 9 years ago, when Lila was in 3rd grade. She had a sparkly backpack covered in unicorn stickers and a habit of hiding things in the picture book bin by the window—once a rock that glowed blue, once a half-eaten lollipop. She forgot to come back for recess. By the time she ran in, crying, Bubbles was flopping on top of *Where the Wild Things Are*. Ms. Mabel didn’t yell. She got a mason jar from her desk, filled it with water from the drinking fountain, and set Bubbles on the windowsill. Lila visited every day after that, bringing little bits of bread for Bubbles. When Bubbles got too big, they put him in the school’s fish tank by the front office. I still see Lila sometimes, now she’s in high school, and she stops to wave at the tank.

Then the Tuesday cookies. Ms. Mabel started leaving half-eaten chocolate chip cookies on the edge of her desk 7 years ago, after the nurse told her to cut back on sugar. She eats half, always a neat little bite mark shaped like a heart, and leaves the rest for me. I know Tuesday before the bell even rings—my feet tingle, I can smell the chocolate through the walls. Sometimes the cookies get a little squishy if a kid spills juice on them, or a custodian knocks one off the desk and it lands in the dust. Once, a 2nd grader named Jake tried to steal my cookie. Late August golden hour, 6:17 PM exactly, the tide pool off Blackrock Beach, Maine, is a glassy mosaic of sun-streaked teal and amber, the air thick with the sharp tang of brine, rotting kelp, and the distant sweet fizz of a soda can half-buried in the sand. This is Mabel’s tide pool—12 years old, a hermit crab with a lopsided carapace crisscrossed with faint barnacle scars, a right claw twice the size of her left (broken at 10 fighting a seagull for a plastic button), antennae thin as fishing line with a tiny kink at the tip from that same fight. She’s waited three full lunar tides for her new shell: a vintage salt shaker, ceramic base chipped at the rim where it slammed into a boulder mid-storm, iridescent glass top that shifts from lavender to emerald when the sun hits it, screw top crusted with a fleck of red sealing wax and faint rust along the threads.

First comes the interior, arranged through the shaker’s 1.2-inch screw-top opening, her trinkets each carrying a memory sharp enough to taste. She lines them up on the rock beside the shaker first, chirping their names in tiny, high-pitched clicks: *Pale Blue* (frosted, chip-edged, found at 7 when she snuck into a human’s picnic blanket and stole it off their edge), *Cloud Green* (lentil-sized, so frosted it looks like condensed sky, found stuck to a dead starfish’s gut at 9), *Heart Clear* (tiny, perfect heart-shaped, found in the mouth of a flounder at 10), *Purple Peri* (tip of a periwinkle shell she ate at 11, spiral mark still visible), *White Peri* (cracked, from her old best friend Gus’s shell before he moved to the deeper pool at 11). She crawls into the shaker first, her body fitting just right—warm from the sun, smelling of old ketchup and salt, the glass cool against her carapace. She tries *Pale Blue* in the center first, shoving it into place with her left claw, but it’s 0.3 inches too tall, blocking the screw top from closing. She huffs (a tiny, bubbly exhalation) and shoves it to the left wall, propping it against a tiny dent in the glass. Next *Heart Clear* goes center, but it rolls immediately, so she shoves *Purple Peri* to its right to wedge it in. *Cloud Green* goes to the right, but it’s too small to stand out, so she tucks *White Peri* behind it, its crack facing inward like a secret. She counts them three times, chirping each name, before crawling back out to twist the screw top closed—three full turns, her lucky number, the rusted metal squeaking like a mouse.

Then the bead. She spots it half-buried in a clump of bright green Ulva lactuca (sea lettuce) 18 inches away: a tiny red plastic bead, the kind from a kid’s friendship bracelet, with a 0.1-inch scratch on its side from being stepped on by a sandal, a hole drilled through its center that glints like a tiny eye. She scuttles toward it, her legs moving at 2 inches per second, until she’s nose-to-snail with Gary, a periwinkle snail with a scratch on his shell from a crab that tried to eat him last month. The argument is exactly 2 minutes, timed by the lapping of the tide: 0:00, Mabel waves her big claw, hissing a sharp, bubbly threat; 0:15, Gary pulls his body into his shell, hissing back; 0:45, Mabel offers *White Peri*—Gus’s shell fragment—holding it for 2.7 seconds longer than she means to, reluctant to give up the last piece of Gus she has; 1:15, Gary hesitates, then slides *White Peri* off his shell; 1:45, Gary pulls the bead out of the algae, his antennae brushing it like a goodbye; 2:00, Mabel grabs the bead, scuttling back to her shaker, triumphant, her legs moving twice as fast as before.

Halfway up the shaker’s side, a strand of Ulva lactuca catches on her right antenna, wrapping tight around the kink. She tries to brush it off with her left claw, but it only twists tighter, the slimy green frond stretching 2.3 inches long, dotted with tiny air bubbles that pop when she touches them. She freezes, tilting her head, and remembers the bride from the wedding she watched last July—white feather hat, veil trailing down one side, tilting her head just like this when the groom kissed her. She adjusts the seaweed, tucking a frond behind her left antenna to make it hang down the side of her head like a veil, and scuttles around the shaker, showing off to Ruby, an 8-year-old hermit crab with a soda can shell who’s picking at a piece of dead kelp. Ruby waves her claw, chirping, and Mabel puffs out her carapace, proud.

She uses a tiny dollop of sticky, slimy Ulva (the kind that acts like crab glue) to stick the red bead to the front of the shaker, right under the chipped rim, centered perfectly. She adds a 0.5-inch piece of white barnacle shell to the left side, and a bent, white plastic fork tine (found last week, half-buried in the sand) to the right. Then she perches on the shaker’s chipped rim, adjusting her position so her big claw hangs over the edge, her little claw gripping the glass for balance, her legs wiggling a little to keep steady. The golden hour sun hits the iridescent glass, turning it pink and blue and green, and the trinkets inside glow through the screw top’s holes like tiny, colorful stars. She chirps three times—her happy chirp—her antennae twitching, the seaweed hat tickling her head.

That’s when the kids come. Three 7-year-olds, Mia, Jax, and Lila, in yellow rain boots covered in dinosaur stickers, even though it’s sunny, carrying a bucket of sea glass and shells, popsicle smudges on their cheeks. Mia spots her first, pointing and yelling so loud the seagulls squawk: “Look! A fairy crab! It has a shiny castle!” Jax leans down, his dirty hand reaching for the shaker, a smudge of blue popsicle on his thumb. Mabel panics, scuttling back into the shaker so fast her legs kick up a tiny splash of water, twisting the screw top closed three more times, her antennae tucked tight against her carapace. She can hear them talking: “It’s magic! It ran!” “Let’s give it a present!” Lila pulls a crumpled blue sour candy wrapper out of her pocket—bright blue, with a picture of a great white shark on it, a tiny tear in the corner where she pulled it open, a smudge of sour candy stuck to the inside. She sets it down next to the shaker, and the kids run off, yelling, “Bye fairy crab!” their voices fading as they climb the dunes.

After 17 seconds of hiding, Mabel peeks out of the shaker, her antennae twitching, and crawls over to the wrapper. She touches it with her antenna, smelling the sharp, sweet tang of sour candy, and chirps softly. Later, when the tide goes out, she’ll stick it to the back of her shaker as a secret decoration, the red bead on the front, the seaweed hat still tickling her head, the trinkets glowing inside her shiny castle.
